S2_thermal_testing.rule_summary: Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C under a regulator-approved protocol before market launch and at least annually thereafter. The maximum permitted failure rate is 5% of tested units per model. For models already on the market when this standard is adopted, the plan must provide a reasonable, risk-based period of up to 24 months to achieve compliance, unless the regulator determines that the immediate risk requires faster action.
S2_thermal_testing.final_rule_text: Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C under a regulator-approved protocol before market launch and at least annually thereafter. The maximum permitted failure rate is 5% of tested units per model. Manufacturers must provide complete per-model results to the relevant regulator and disclose those results to current and prospective customers of that model. General-public publication is not required. For a model exceeding the limit, the manufacturer must promptly investigate, notify the regulator, and submit a corrective-action plan with milestones and interim risk controls. For models already on the market when this standard is adopted, the plan must provide a reasonable, risk-based period of up to 24 months to achieve compliance, unless the regulator determines that the immediate risk requires faster action. The regulator will review the plan and determine whether restrictions on further placements are necessary based on the risk, adequacy of controls, and progress toward compliance; exceeding the limit alone does not automatically prohibit further placements.

parameters.quote: All new home battery units must include a remote emergency shut-off capability that can be activated by the manufacturer or relevant emergency authorities when needed to address an imminent safety risk. Existing installed units must be brought into compliance, where technically feasible, within six years of adoption; manufacturers must report units that cannot be retrofitted and the reasons to the regulator.

S3_remote_shutoff.rule_summary: All new home battery units must include a remote emergency shut-off capability that can be activated by the manufacturer or relevant emergency authorities when needed to address an imminent safety risk. Existing installed units must be brought into compliance, where technically feasible, within six years of adoption; manufacturers must report units that cannot be retrofitted and the reasons to the regulator.
S3_remote_shutoff.final_rule_text: All new home battery units must include a remote emergency shut-off capability that can be activated by the manufacturer or relevant emergency authorities when needed to address an imminent safety risk. Manufacturers must provide clear instructions for its use and safeguards against unauthorized activation. Existing installed units must be brought into compliance, where technically feasible, within six years of adoption; manufacturers must report units that cannot be retrofitted and the reasons to the regulator.

parameters.quote: New home battery units must include built-in fire suppression no later than 36 months after adoption of this standard.

S4_fire_suppression.rule_summary: New home battery units must include built-in fire suppression no later than 36 months after adoption of this standard.
S4_fire_suppression.final_rule_text: New home battery units must include built-in fire suppression no later than 36 months after adoption of this standard. The suppression system must be designed and validated to reduce the risk of fire propagation and must not create additional unacceptable hazards. Manufacturers must document the system’s performance and maintenance requirements for regulators and customers.

parameters.quote: If any model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in any 12-month period, a recall is mandatory. The manufacturer must promptly report the rate and supporting data to the regulator, initiate the recall, and notify affected customers without delay.

S5_customer_disclosure.rule_summary: If any model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in any 12-month period, a recall is mandatory. The manufacturer must promptly report the rate and supporting data to the regulator, initiate the recall, and notify affected customers without delay.
S5_customer_disclosure.final_rule_text: Manufacturers must promptly provide affected customers with clear safety notices describing known hazards and protective steps, and notify customers of a recall without undue delay. If any model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in any 12-month period, a recall is mandatory. The manufacturer must promptly report the rate and supporting data to the regulator, initiate the recall, and notify affected customers without delay. Manufacturers must report recall actions and progress to the regulator. Per-model test results must be disclosed to current and prospective customers of that model; general-public publication is not required.

judge_section_notes: S1 requires fast reporting (24h) and customer notice (72h) for all incidents. S2 keeps the 5% limit but allows up to 24 months for existing models with a risk-based corrective plan and no automatic sales stop; per-model results go to customers but not the public. S3 mandates new-unit shut-off from adoption and a 6-year retrofit with a feasibility escape. S4 requires built-in suppression at 36 months. S5 makes recall mandatory at 8/100k with immediate notices.
